title: Raga Suhi
hook: a raga of union and weddings that opens with a clean vessel, a pot of milk and a churn

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Tilang, sung to Lalo, and your line was truth to power. Did a moment come for your one true sentence? Day one thousand ninety-four.

A steel pot on the kitchen counter, a dish towel over the lid, left alone for the night. Warm milk went in. A spoonful of yesterday's yogurt went in after it. By morning the two have become one thing, thick and set, and nobody can pull them apart again. Punjabi kitchens know that pot. The Guru Granth Sahib knows it too. Today's raga is tied by tradition to weddings and union, and the very first hymn in its section isn't about a bride at all. It's about the pot. Today: Raga Suhi.
screen: `A POT LEFT FOR THE NIGHT.` → `TWO BECOME ONE THING.` → `A RAGA OF UNION OPENS IN A KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Suhi follows Tilang in the Granth's order, opening on ang seven twenty-eight. Sikh tradition links it with union and with weddings, and its pages hold songs of the bride and the beloved; tomorrow we'll open some of them. Second, the kitchen. Guru Nanak's opening hymn, in paraphrase: wash the vessel, sit down, purify it with incense, and only then go out for the milk. The milk is your deeds. Awareness is the culture you stir in. And set it free of craving for a reward. Third, the refrain, the line the hymn keeps returning to: chant the one Name; every other work bears no fruit. Fourth, the churn. Make this mind the handles, the hymn says, and staying awake the cord. Let the tongue repeat the Name, and churn like that: this is how the nectar is found. Now see why a raga of union might begin here. Milk and culture become one thing only in a clean pot, left in peace, without anyone poking at it to see if it's ready yet. The hymn describes union the way a cook does: prepare the vessel, bring something good, add a little of what's alive, and wait without grasping. Then the churning, the patient work that brings out what was hidden inside. Some readers hear in this the soul and God becoming one. Others hear a plain daily discipline. Both start with the same instruction: wash the pot first. That's today's line. Union.
screen: `SUHI FOLLOWS TILANG.` · `WASH THE VESSEL, THEN FETCH THE MILK.` · `CHANT THE ONE NAME.` · `THE MIND AS THE CHURN'S HANDLES.` · then, large: `UNION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Suhi, or wash the vessel. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Suhi. Either way, sit and let the breath slow. For the first minute, wash the pot: let go of whatever's still sloshing around from today, one thing at a time, without arguing with it. For the second minute, leave it be. Don't check on yourself. Don't ask whether it's working. Just sit, like milk left to set. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the one word you stir in. If you don't, let the breath be enough. The bell holds the time.
Raga Suhi. The raga after Tilang, linked by tradition with weddings and union, which opens with a clean vessel, milk, a little culture and a churn. Today's word.
Your line: union. Today, before one thing that matters, a meal, a call, a conversation, clear the vessel first: one breath, hands still, and then begin. Day one thousand ninety-four.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Suhi section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Suhi, and because Suhi holds the Lavan, the raga is heard at the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding.

original.note: suhi, the raga after Tilang, linked by tradition with weddings and union.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wedding raga is about the wedding.
what it means: Suhi opens with a kitchen: a clean vessel, milk of good deeds, awareness stirred in, set without craving.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's first Suhi hymn (ang 728) maps the whole dairy process, washing, setting and churning, onto devotion, with the refrain japahu ta eko nama, chant the one Name.
recall: a musical instruction in the heading

sources.ref: Suhi Mahalla 1, Ang 728 (bhaanda dhoe bais dhoop devhu; milk as deeds, awareness as culture, set without craving; refrain japahu ta eko nama; the mind as the churn's handles, wakefulness as the cord)
Suhi Mahalla 4, the Lavan, Ang 773 (mentioned only)

notes: Paraphrase of Suhi Mahalla 1, Ang 728: bhaanda dhoe bais dhoop devhu tau doodhai kau jaavahu; doodh karam phun surat samaain hoe niraas jamaavahu; japahu ta eko nama, avar niraphal kaama (rahao); ihu man eetee haath karahu phun netrau need na aavai; rasna naam japahu tab matheeai, in bidh amrit paavahu. Please confirm the paraphrase, especially 'eetee' (churn handles) and 'netrau' (churning cord).
'Sikh tradition links it with union and weddings' follows the outline; the raga-mood claim is attributed to tradition.
'Punjabi kitchens know that pot' is an everyday description, not a claim about how many.
howItsDone says the Lavan are in Suhi and sung at the Anand Karaj, per the Sikh Rehat Maryada.
Editor pass: varied the teach opener; fixed the fork setup, which said the milk was ready while the answer was to fetch it.
